master.title: Sunday Crunch: Ukraine high alert
master.content:
Press play to listen to this article

Presented by Electronic Arts.

By ANNABELLE DICKSON

PRESENTED BY

Send tips here | Subscribe for free | Listen to Sunday Crunch and view in your browser

3 THINGS TO KNOW

UKRAINE HIGH ALERT: An “imminent” Russian invasion of Ukraine is “entirely possible,” Cabinet minister Brandon Lewis said this morning as tensions with Moscow ratchet up ahead of what could be a monumental week.

Lewis added his voice to warnings on both sides of the Atlantic that an attack could come soon. While the U.K. hopes for a “diplomatic outcome,” it’s now a realistic possibility “something much more tragic could occur,” the Northern Ireland secretary told Sky’s Trevor Phillips.

Munich warning: The most eye-catching and controversial of the multiple downbeat assessments of the situation from Western leaders over the weekend was Defense Secretary Ben Wallace’s comments to the Sunday Times. “It may be that he [Putin] just switches off his tanks and we all go home but there is a whiff of Munich in the air from some in the West.”

Interpretation: Lewis insisted Wallace was not talking about appeasement of the Nazis, despite almost everyone seeing it that way. The reference was to the “optimism at the time” that there “may be a diplomatic way through, that eventually proved to not be the case … because it turned out that wasn’t the intent or the aim of Adolf Hitler at the time,” Lewis told the BBC.

**A message from Electronic Arts: Electronic Arts and Internet Matters partnered up to help parents make smart choices about their children’s video game playing. Learn about the great results of the campaign here.**

Not going down very well: The Royal United Services Institute’s Russia expert Mark Galeotti told Sky’s Phillips that the comments were “unfortunate, not least, because it obviously casts the Russians as Nazi Germany.” For a country “which lost so much in the second world war, which still calls it the great patriotic war” it was a “very neuralgic point,” he said.

Over in the U.S.: Joe Biden spoke to Vladimir Putin for about an hour yesterday after the U.S. warned Americans “it’s past time to leave” a potential war zone. Senior adviser to Biden Derek Chollet told the BBC’s Sophie Raworth that a Russian “military incursion” into Ukraine could come “at any day,” and warned if Putin chooses the path of escalation and confrontation there will be “swift and severe consequences.”

Wednesday watch: American officials told POLITICO that intelligence suggests Russia could invade on Wednesday. Lewis told the BBC he would not go into intelligence findings, but said it was clear that where the Russians had amassed troops they had the “ability to move very quickly.”

False flag claim: Moscow is preparing to “create the circumstances” in which it could justify an invasion on the grounds that Russian troops are “responding to Ukrainian or Western aggression,” a Whitehall source tells the Sunday Telegraph.

What happens next? Of course the big question is what would happen in the event Putin does make a move. Chollet said economic sanctions imposed by the West would be “crippling” to the Russian economy, and that the U.S. is prepared to bolster its military capacity on NATO’s eastern flank.

Regret coming? Asked on the BBC if the U.K. might regret not sending in troops, Lewis again stressed Ukraine is not a part of NATO. Former head of the army Richard Dannatt told Times Radio: “I’m afraid I’m being hard-hearted here — it’s their fight, not our fight. We will support them of course, but it’s their fight.”

Would you evacuate? Labour warned over the weekend that ministers should learn lessons from the chaos of the Afghanistan evacuation to help people fleeing Ukraine. Lewis told Raworth it was “different situation” in Afghanistan, with allied forces criticized for a chaotic evacuation amid a quicker-than-expected Taliban advance. “Not least because of the abilities and the weaponry and the measures that Russia have compared to what the Taliban had,” he added.

Sub-tweeting Dominic Raab? In absolutely no way trying to score political points against a certain Cabinet colleague, cough, Wallace announced this morning he is returning from a planned long weekend abroad with his family.

Mentioning no names: In her own BBC interview, Shadow Home Secretary Yvette Cooper insisted Labour party had “always” supported NATO despite “different leader views in the past.”

Thread klaxon: Tory foreign affairs committee chairman Tom Tugendhat has just fired out this punchy Twitter thread on all the steps short of war he reckons Britain should be taking to pile real pressure on Moscow in the coming days.

Expert view: Russia expert Galeotti told Sky’s Trevor Phillips that Western leaders must make clear that there are “off-ramps” for Russia. Given a binary option between escalation and capitulation, Putin will probably escalate. The Russian leader needs to feel there is a genuine step forward for him, the RUSI wonk added.  “Do I think there is going to be a war on Wednesday? I will say not,” Galeotti predicted. Something to cling on to on a Sunday afternoon.

2. BATTLE FOR THE MET: The fallout from the dramatic resignation of Metropolitan Police chief Cressida Dick last week continues, with City Hall and the Home Office running separate briefing operations about the row.

Stay out of it: On Marsham Street, Home Secretary Priti Patel is “looking at all options” to bar London mayor Sadiq Khan from having any say in appointing Scotland Yard’s next leader, the Sunday Times reports. Ex-National Crime Agency boss Lynne Owens is Patel’s preferred candidate if she puts herself forward, the paper also reckons. Asked about the anti-Khan briefings this morning, Lewis claimed on Sky it was “always best to avoid getting involved with rumors.”

Price of support: Khan makes it clear in an Observer article he’s ready to flex his muscles on the appointment. “I will not support the appointment of a new commissioner unless they can clearly demonstrate that they understand the scale of the cultural problems within the Met and the urgency with which they must be addressed,” he warns.

Perfect storm: Cooper told the BBC policing now faces a “perfect storm” — and she wants reform beyond just the Met. “Crime is going up, prosecutions are going down and confidence is falling,” she told Raworth.

Now read this: The Observer has a nice piece asking five experts if the Met can really change.

3. RED MEAT FOR THE RIGHT: The PM’s new chief of staff has some juicy red meat for the Conservative right this weekend. He’s penned a Sunday Telegraph op-ed pledging to “step back” from people’s lives and pursue “a smaller state.” He said it’s time for “a more enabling approach” after the big interventions of the pandemic.

Maths be damned: Lewis followed up by telling Sky the PM had his “100 percent plus loyalty.” He added of Johnson: “This is a prime minister who is doing the right things for our country, he has got the big decisions right. I think he will fight and he will win as a result of that the next general election.”

But but but: Lewis repeatedly insisted questions about whether he would continue to serve if Johnson was found to have broken the rules were “hypothetical.” Lewis also told the BBC he had not got a questionnaire from the police, as Downing Street announced the prime minister had last week.

IDS of march: Quite a contrast with former Tory leader Iain Duncan Smith who told the i that the PM would find it “very tough” to remain in office if police conclude that he broke the rules.

Someone check in with Dilyn: Cabinet minister Nadine Dorries declared she will stay by Johnson’s side even if he is fined. But, er, “if he went up and, you know, kicked a dog, I’d probably withdraw my support for him,” she told CNN.

If all that fails: The Sunday Times gives Rishi Sunak the Tim Shipman treatment. The chancellor really does look like a contender after allies let it be known he “drinks exclusively Yorkshire tea, is a devotee of the pork and apple pie from Kitson & Sons butchers in Northallerton” and is often heard to say “now then” and “job’s a good ’un” around Downing Street. A real man of the people.

Happy right: Voice of the Tory right the Sunday Express quotes an “insider” who says that after the PM’s mini reshuffle last week there is “more confidence that the benefits of Brexit will be delivered upon.” They tell the paper: “If you look at the reshuffle, former chairman of the European Research Group [Chris Heaton-Harris] is chief whip, Jacob Rees-Mogg has a cabinet position dedicated to Brexit. It’s been a good week for Brexiters.”

Speaking of whom: David Frost, Johnson’s former Brexit negotiator who quit last year with a blast at Johnson’s direction of travel, is among those who have written a joint letter to the PM insisting it is “time to reverse” the ban on mining shale gas in place since 2019. The Sunday Telegraph has the story.

But but but: Minister Zac Goldsmith is not sounding impressed.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING

CRY FOR HELP: Labour MP Rosie Duffield gave an excoriating assessment of Labour leader Keir Starmer’s approach to tackling local activist’s harassment of her, even suggesting she had been “tempted” to defect to the Conservatives. A write up of the interview made Saturday’s Telegraph. Cooper told the BBC she’s spoken to Duffield and that Starmer has made it clear there should not be abuse of any kind.

NO GOING BACK: “It will be impossible to go back [into the EU] because our economy will be so transformed that firstly nobody would want to and secondly the EU would look at us in horror because we would not be following all their petty rules,” Jacob Rees Mogg tells the Sunday Express in his first interview as the PM’s Brexit opportunities minister.

STORMONT CLOUDS GATHERING: Brandon Lewis told the BBC’s Raworth he will be in Northern Ireland in the “next few days” after coming under fire for going to Washington last week in the middle of the big Stormont crisis. He also said he believed there was a “landing ground” for resolving the dispute over the Northern Ireland Protocol.

APPOINTMENT: Leveling-up Cabinet minister Michael Gove has appointed Paul Collier, who the Indy says is a “controversial professor who suggested non-white British-born people are not ‘indigenous’.”

POWER OF TWITTER: Campaigner Jack Monroe returned to her local Asda to find that her Twitter campaign, highlighting the spiraling prices of the cheapest groceries, has been successful.

WATCH OUT FOR NEXT WEEK

WASHINGTON BOUND: While Westminster is quiet as MPs enjoy a parliamentary recess, Tory Party Chairman Oliver Dowden will take the war on woke to Washington (though not sure they need loads of help with this stuff.) The Mail on Sunday has a preview of his speech to the Heritage Foundation and says he will also meet Republican election strategists.

LEAVING THE BUBBLE: The PM will leave SW1 and spend recess week promoting the government’s leveling up plans (read: dodging questions on Partygate). His first stop is expected to be Scotland tomorrow — a bit awks when so many senior Tories north of the border, including the Scottish Tory leader Douglas Ross, have called for him to go. Sky has the details.

GRAB A COFFEE AND READ

DIPLOMACY FAIL: “All [the West’s leaders and diplomats] think that when they go to Russia, they are talking to people whose minds can be changed by argument or debate. They think the Russian elite cares about things like its ‘reputation.’ It does not,” Anne Applebaum’s look at why the West’s diplomacy with Russia keeps failing in the Atlantic is both depressing and informative. It is also pretty brutal in its assessment of U.K. Foreign Secretary Liz Truss.

CRICK DOORSTEPPED: The Observer’s Tim Adams doorsteps Michael Crick — king of the ambush as political editor of BBC’s Newsnight and as political correspondent at Channel 4 News. Crick’s new book — ‘One Party After Another’ — is actually about Nigel Farage and not just a readout of the No.10 grid for 2020.

HOW TOPPLE A PM: POLITICO’s Jack Blanchard looks into the murky world of leadership challenges and asks what it’s like to topple a prime minister on his Westminster Insider podcast this week. Among his guests, Former Aussie PM Malcolm Turnbull recalls the internal coup which ended his premiership in 2018.

SUNDAY MEDIA ROUND

Carole Walker (sitting in for Ayesha Hazarika) on Times Radio, 4 p.m. to 7 p.m.:  Labour MP Justin Madders; SNP MP Dave Doogan; Conservative MP Matt Warman; the Express’s deputy pol ed Sam Lister and Harry Potter star Rupert Grint.

Westminster Hour, BBC Radio 4, 10 p.m.: Conservative MP Kevin Hollinrake; Shadow Cabinet Office Minister Fleur Anderson; pollster James Johnson and the i’s Hugo Gye.

WEEK AHEAD

MONDAY

The Commons and Lords are in recess all week.

ANYONE FOR CAKE? It’s the second anniversary of Rishi Sunak becoming chancellor.

PM IN SCOTLAND: Boris Johnson takes leveling up on tour.

TRANSATLANTIC: Oliver Dowden addresses the Heritage Foundation and meets Republican election strategists in Washington.

WEDNESDAY

INFLATION: Latest Retail Price Index from the Office for National Statistics, 7 a.m.

FRIDAY

ECONOMIC RECOVERY: Latest retail sales stats from the ONS, 7 a.m.

Thanks: To Matt Honeycombe-Foster for bringing humor and editing prowess to Sunday Crunch.

**A message from Electronic Arts: The Play Together/Play Smart campaign from Internet Matters and Electronic Arts aims to help more parents set up parental controls on the video games their children play. Of those parents the campaign reached, a majority (55%) acted and set up parental controls on their children’s games console. This increased to three-fifths (61%) among those who had recently purchased a games console in the run up to Christmas. EA believes that parental controls, coupled with an ongoing and open discussion within the family about play time, spend, age-appropriate games and online behavior, can help ensure that children enjoy a positive experience while playing video games.**

candidate.title: Why the West’s Diplomacy With Russia Keeps Failing
candidate.content:
Oh, how I envy Liz Truss her opportunity! Oh, how I regret her utter failure to make use of it! For those who have never heard of her, Truss is the lightweight British foreign secretary who went to Moscow this week to tell her Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, that his country should not invade Ukraine. This trip was not a success. At a glacial press conference he likened their conversation to “the mute” speaking with “the deaf”; later, he leaked the fact that she had confused some Russian regions with Ukrainian regions, to add a little insult to the general injury.

Lavrov has done this many times before. He was vile to the European Union’s foreign-policy chief, Josep Borrell, last year. He has been unpleasant at international conferences and rude to journalists. His behavior is not an accident. Lavrov, like Russian President Vladimir Putin, uses aggression and sarcasm as tools to demonstrate his scorn for his interlocutor, to frame negotiations as useless even before they begin, to create dread and apathy. The point is to put other diplomats on the defensive, or else to cause them to give up in disgust.

But the fact that Lavrov is disrespectful and disagreeable is old news. So is the fact that Putin lectures foreign leaders for hours and hours on his personal and political grievances. He did that the first time he met President Barack Obama, more than a decade ago; he did exactly the same thing last week to French President Emmanuel Macron. Truss should have known all of this. Instead of offering empty language about rules and values, she could have started the press conference like this:

Good evening, ladies and gentlemen of the press. I am delighted to join you after meeting my Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov. This time, we have not bothered to discuss treaties he won’t respect and promises he won’t keep. We have told him, instead, that an invasion of Ukraine will carry very, very high costs—higher than he has ever imagined. We are now planning to cut off Russian gas exports completely—Europe will find its energy supplies somewhere else. We are now preparing to assist the Ukrainian resistance, for a decade if need be. We are quadrupling our support for the Russian opposition, and for Russian media too. We want to make sure that Russians will start hearing the truth about this invasion, and as loudly as possible. And if you want to do regime change in Ukraine, we’ll get to work on regime change in Russia.

Truss, or Borrell before her, could have added just a touch of personal insult, in the style of Lavrov himself, and wondered out loud just how it is that Lavrov’s official salary pays for the lavish properties that his family makes use of in London. She could have listed the names of the many other Russian public servants who send their children to schools in Paris or Lugano. She could have announced that these children are now, all of them, on their way home, along with their parents: No more American School in Switzerland! No more pied-à-terres in Knightsbridge! No more Mediterranean yachts!

Of course Truss—like Borrell, like Macron, like the German chancellor who is headed for Moscow this week—would never say anything like this, not even in private. Tragically, the Western leaders and diplomats who are right now trying to stave off a Russian invasion of Ukraine still think they live in a world where rules matter, where diplomatic protocol is useful, where polite speech is valued. All of them think that when they go to Russia, they are talking to people whose minds can be changed by argument or debate. They think the Russian elite cares about things like its “reputation.” It does not.

Read: The reason Putin would risk war

In fact, when talking to the new breed of autocrats, whether in Russia, China, Venezuela, or Iran, we are now dealing with something very different: people who aren’t interested in treaties and documents, people who only respect hard power. Russia is in violation of the Budapest Memorandum, signed in 1994, guaranteeing Ukrainian security. Do you ever hear Putin talk about that? Of course not. He isn’t concerned about his untrustworthy reputation either: Lying keeps opponents on their toes. Nor does Lavrov mind if he is hated, because hatred gives him an aura of power.

Their intentions are different from ours too. Putin’s goal is not a flourishing, peaceful, prosperous Russia, but a Russia where he remains in charge. Lavrov’s goal is to maintain his position in the murky world of the Russian elite and, of course, to keep his money. What we mean by “interests” and what they mean by “interests” are not the same. When they listen to our diplomats, they don’t hear anything that really threatens their position, their power, their personal fortunes.

Despite all of our talk, no one has ever seriously tried to end, rather than simply limit, Russian money laundering in the West, or Russian political or financial influence in the West. No one has taken seriously the idea that Germans should now make themselves independent of Russian gas, or that France should ban political parties that accept Russian money, or that the U.K. and the U.S. should stop Russian oligarchs from buying property in London or Miami. No one has suggested that the proper response to Putin’s information war on our political system would be an information war on his.

Read: The U.S. is naive about Russia. Ukraine can’t afford to be.

Now we are on the brink of what could be a catastrophic conflict. American, British, and European embassies in Ukraine are evacuating; citizens have been warned to leave. But this terrible moment represents not just a failure of diplomacy; it also reflects a failure of the Western imagination, a generation-long refusal, on the part of diplomats, politicians, journalists, and intellectuals, to understand what kind of state Russia was becoming and to prepare accordingly. We have refused to see the representatives of this state for what they are. We have refused to speak to them in a way that might have mattered. Now it might be too late.

llm_judgement.note: Different outlets and authors; one is a Politico newsletter on UK reactions to possible Russian invasion of Ukraine, the other is an Atlantic opinion essay on Western diplomacy with Russia.
